title: What manner of love (1 John 3:1–3)
hook: see what love: that we should be called children of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elder's pet name, and your line was little children. Who got your note that began, I'm writing because? Day six hundred eighty-five.

Somewhere in a lot of families there's a box. Inside: crayon drawings, a first shoe, a report card, a lock of hair. Plenty of people only find it as adults, clearing out a closet, and it stops them cold: someone kept all of this, because it was mine. A love they never saw, kept the whole time. Today's passage is only three verses long, and it begins with that kind of surprise. The writer of First John has been talking about light and darkness, sin and commandments. Then he stops, as if he's suddenly overcome, and says: look.

In the King James Bible: "Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God." Behold. Look at this. What manner of love: the Greek phrase carries surprise, something like, what kind of love is this? Where does love like this even come from? Bestowed is a gift word. Not earned. Given. And the gift is a name: called children of God. Here's a detail from the manuscripts. The oldest Greek manuscripts add three more words after that line, and so we are. Called children of God, and so we are. The manuscripts behind the King James didn't have those words, and modern translations usually put them back. It's as if the writer heard the word called and worried someone would think it was only a title. It isn't only a title. It's what you are. Then he adds why the world doesn't always see it: "therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not." If people missed who Jesus was, they'll miss who his children are too. Then the future, and here he admits what he doesn't know: "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be." Now. Already. But not yet finished. We don't know what we'll be. What we do know, he says, is that when he appears, "we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is." And the last verse says hope like that changes how you live now: whoever has this hope purifies himself.
screen: `BEHOLD: WHAT KIND OF LOVE IS THIS?`
`NOW, BUT NOT YET WHAT WE SHALL BE.`
`WE SHALL SEE HIM AS HE IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear a kinder name. Settle, and breathe. Think of the names you call yourself in a hard moment. Failure. Idiot. Too much. Not enough. Notice them without arguing. Then, slowly, set beside them the name the letter uses: children of God. If you pray, you can hear it with your own name in front of it. If that phrase isn't yours, try a plainer one: I am loved. Notice what happens in your body. Rest there, and just look. The bell holds the time.
What manner of love. The wonder of First John: love so surprising that we're called children of God, and so we are.
Your line: children of god. Today, each time you hear yourself use a harsh name for yourself, notice it, and set a kinder one beside it. Day six hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Many Christians read 1 John 3:1–2 at baptisms and on All Saints' Day, and the line about seeing God as he is shapes Christian hope in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teaching alike.

myth: the KJV includes the words 'and so we are' in 3:1
the manuscripts behind the KJV lacked them. the oldest Greek manuscripts have them.
the writer admits we don't yet know what we shall be
"it doth not yet appear what we shall be."
being called children of God is only a title here
the writer insists: called, and so we are.

fork.setup: you're the writer. you've just said believers are called children of God. how do you make sure no one hears it as only a title?
options: explain what a name means in law.
fork.reveal: the oldest manuscripts read, called children of God, and so we are. not only a name: a fact.

original.note: Greek: what kind of, what sort of, often with a note of wonder. the word behind 'what manner of'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet verse about God loving everyone.
what it means: a gift of belonging so surprising the writer says 'look', already true now, with more not yet seen.
what a scholar hears: 'and so we are' (kai esmen) is in the oldest manuscripts but missing from the KJV's Greek text; and potapēn, a word of wonder.

notes: καὶ ἐσμέν ('and so we are') in 3:1 is in the major early manuscripts (e.g. Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus) and absent from the Textus Receptus behind the KJV. Confirm.
KJV 'sons of God' (Greek τέκνα, children); the carry 'children of god' follows the Greek. Confirm.
ποταπός as 'of what sort', with a note of wonder; the older derivation 'from what country' is uncertain and is not used.
Use of 1 John 3:1–3 on All Saints' Day (it is a reading in several lectionaries) and at baptisms: confirm.
The carry's lowercase 'god' follows the index exactly; the spoken voice says it naturally.

Audit (second sample): hook used an adoption hearing, a belonging image that repeats day 684's family pet names and fits Paul's adoption language better than First John's (which speaks of being born of God); now a kept box of childhood things. Cut stock lines ('a detail scholars love', 'Christians across traditions have treasured this line'). Practice and carry no longer tell the listener to call themselves a child of God; it is offered 'if you pray', with a plain alternative.
